title: Self-Authority
author: Cindy Chance
summary: Chance distinguishes self-authority, a habit of character that claims ownership of decisions within one's own domain, from both confidence and control, arguing it is frequently mistaken for either but functions differently from both. She contends that visible control-seeking and excessive deference are not opposites but two extremes that arise when self-authority has not been established, both driven by an underlying anxiety about facing a decision directly. Chance connects the concept to psychologist Robert Kegan's self-authoring stage of adult development, framing self-authority as the capacity to decide what story one is living without confusing it with someone else's story, while still respecting the boundary of others' authority over their own decisions. She closes by reframing the entire question away from certainty, positioning self-authority as an act of claiming responsibility rather than a state of confident knowledge.
points: Chance's key distinction, self-authority is being sure of who gets to make it, not being sure of a decision (confidence), separates two concepts commonly conflated in leadership writing.

She reframes both micromanaging control and excessive deference as the same underlying failure, two extremes that arise when self-authority has not been established, both driven by anxiety rather than opposite temperaments.

Grounding the concept in Robert Kegan's adult-development theory of self-authoring gives the essay a research anchor beyond personal observation, connecting it to a broader psychological framework of maturity.
The closing reframe, replacing are you certain with are you willing, shifts the practical takeaway from a cognitive test to a volitional one.
quotes: Self-authority might be mistaken for confidence, because confident people often seem to have it. But it is something quite different. Confidence is being sure of a decision. Self-authority is being sure of who gets to make it.

Watch a controlling boss and a people-pleasing employee in the same meeting. They look like opposites, one seizing opportunities, one disappearing into the views of others, but they are both reacting.
Deference and control in the face of others' authority are not opposites. They are two extremes that arise when self-authority has not been established.
Self-authority recognizes the authority of others as much as the authority of self. It has to, that's what makes it a boundary and not just a claim.

On one reading, self-authority is the moral-psychological cousin of what Robert Kegan calls self-authoring in his stages of adult development, the capacity not just to hold values, but to step outside the systems and relationships that were handed you as your values, and choose among them for yourself.
So the question isn't whether you're certain. It's whether you're willing, to claim what's yours, to leave what isn't, and to bear all that entails.
